newsitem.title: USA: Coffee prices drop on profit-taking, gold falls.
newsitem.headline: Coffee prices drop on profit-taking, gold falls.

text.p: Coffee prices fell sharply on Monday as speculators exited positions held in the expiring May futures contract, sparking a round of profit-taking from last week's run-up to 20-year highs.
At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, coffee for May delivery expired at 255.25 cents, down 21.25 cents on the day.

It touched its life-of-contract high at 280 cents -- also the highest price since June 1977 -- in early trading before a wave of liquidation ahead of the noon expiry prompted a price collapse. July coffee ended at 246.25 cents, down 6.90.

Traders said talk that world coffee producers now meeting in London might opt to suspend a scheme of export quotas in order to keep coffee prices competitive with other beverages might have helped spur the selloff.
"There's a concern that as the market approaches $3.00 you start to impact consumption," said Dean Witter analyst Steve Platt. "And producers don't want to shut off consumption."

Platt said Colombia's announcement late on Friday that it was reopening registrations for coffee exports for May and June shipment may also have fed selling, including some sales of futures by producer nations to secure a high price.
Colombian officials had said last week they were having great difficulty finding supplies to satisfy export needs.

Coffee prices have soared since December on a variety of factors that have prompted supply worries, including smaller crops in Central America and Colombia, tight stocks at U.S. coffee roasters, and strikes delaying Colombian shipments.
The market remains concerned about possible cold weather damage in Brazil, the top grower, as that nation heads into its winter months in June and July.

Citing higher world green coffee prices, Procter and Gamble unit Folgers Coffee Co on Monday raised the list price for its standard 13-ounce can of ground regular coffee by 30 cents to $3.36, the fourth rise since February and a jump of almost 50 percent since then.
"Consumers are not yet complaining about the price of coffee," said Donald Schoenholt, president of Brooklyn-based roaster Gilles Coffee. "But I believe that's going to change."

In other markets, gold prices continued to fall as traders fretted about Germany's plan to revalue its central bank gold reserves and a possible interest rate rise this week by the Federal Reserve's policy-making Open Market Committee.
June gold on the COMEX ended $2.70 lower at $342.20 an ounce.

"I don't think Germany will sell any gold, but so many people feel that if the rest of the European banks fudge their balance sheets, then there may be additional central bank gold sales," said one New York bullion dealer.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, oil prices fell sharply as traders took profits after a sharp rally on Friday which occurred despite evidence of rising oil supplies.
Crude oil for June delivery closed down 53 cents a barrel at $21.59, with June gasoline ending down 0.66 cent a gallon at 65.21 cents and June heating oil down 0.55 cent a gallon at 57.92 cents.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, wheat prices rose after Egypt bought 200,000 metric tons of U.S. wheat over the weekend. July wheat ended at $3.94-3/4, up 6 cents a bushel.
